text: After summiting, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors. Make one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then a second, loose and dirty one into the moat at the base of the notch. Navigate the crevasse field on Chickamin Glacier to return to base camp.
runs: the moat at the base of the notch

text: A short warm-up leads to the base of the twin cracks. An alternative start begins in the moat at the foot of the Middle-South notch: turn the outside corner, traverse right 30-40 ft, climb a corner, then traverse again to the twin cracks. This start lets a party leave axes and crampons at the base instead of carrying them over.
runs: leads to the base of the twin cracks

text: Rappel 2 of 2, double-rope, into the moat at the base of the notch.
runs: the moat at the base of the notch

text: A first-hand report of the East Face 5.10d describes one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then one more — loose, dirty and cold — into the moat at the base of the notch. The figure of about four rappels on a single 60 m rope is arithmetic from roughly 100 m of descent rather than a published count.
runs: the moat at the base of the notch

text: Access via SR-20 north of Cascade Loop; drive past the hairpin turn just east of Washington Pass to the pullout near Milepost 166 on the south side of the highway. A climbers trail drops from the pullout, immediately crosses Early Winters Creek, and ascends steeply through timbered terrain to a bench camp around 6,500 feet. From camp, continue east toward the Wine Spires. From the bench camp, traverse to approach Chablis Spire via Burgundy Col approach (recommended spring-fall; 2-5 hours total from trailhead) or via Silver Star Creek drainage (recommended for winter; approach in snow). Chablis is reached after traversing past or over Burgundy Col area.
runs: past the hairpin turn just east of washington pass to the

text: East Face, 5-6 pitch route on the east side of the Liberty Bell group.
runs: on the east side of the liberty bell group

text: From the top, one option is to traverse a short catwalk and build rappel anchors roughly 100 feet west of the true summit; another option is to rappel north until you can cross the gully separating Minuteman from Liberty Bell, then downclimb to a bush anchor for a final rappel. Either way, about three rappels on a single 60m rope typically regain the approach talus. Existing fixed slings around horns/blocks should be inspected (and backed up if in doubt) before weighting, since they're exposed to UV and rockfall.
runs: until you can cross the gully separating minuteman from liberty bell then

text: A short pitch of hard ~45-degree glacier ice and a bergschrund/moat crossing guard the base of the East Face; crampons and axe required, and the moat widens as the season progresses.
runs: a short pitch of hard 45 degree glacier ice

text: A short traverse across a small heathered ledge into an exposed, pleasant fourth-class face.
runs: a short traverse across a small heathered ledge

text: An obvious deep low-fifth-class chimney that tops out just a few feet from the summit cairn.
runs: low fifth class chimney that tops out just a few feet from the summit cairn

text: Established over 3 days in September 2008 by Alan Kearney and Erik Johnson (a route Kearney had attempted in 1991 and 2003), the line follows the peak's northeast buttress up compact gneiss with few natural crack systems. The pair placed small cams and numerous knifeblade and bugaboo pitons for protection and drilled no bolts; the route is described as featuring dark, brooding overhangs, a delicate traverse, sections of blank rock, and loose, teetering blocks near the top.
runs: placed small cams and numerous knifeblade and bugaboo pitons

text: A roughly two-day approach traveling via the remnants of the McMillan Creek glaciers to reach the base of the peak's north side/northeast buttress; on the day of the climb the party hiked about 3.5 hours from a high camp to the base of the wall.
runs: the remnants of the mcmillan creek glaciers to

text: From camp, traverse benches, trending slightly downhill, to the outlet of the glacial lake near 5,500 ft. Cross the outlet, climb slabs and snow onto the Terror Glacier, and head for the gully that rises to the col between West and East McMillan Spires.
runs: trending slightly downhill to the outlet of the glacial lake

text: Climbs the east end of Steeple Rock, scrambling along the south side of the ridge to a tree just below the summit. Short, low-angle, and often combined with a harder line as an up-and-over.
runs: the east end of steeple rock scrambling along the

text: Advanced -- an experienced alpine rock party comfortable soloing sustained 4th/low-5th terrain for hours; the published route notes state plainly that if you think you need more specific beta, this is likely not the route for you.
runs: if you think you need more specific beta this is likely not the route for you

text: The route's namesake crux: a sustained 30m hand-and-fist splitter climbed around a small roof and into the crack, finished with a thrilling rightward traverse on face holds to gain a corner crack near the belay.
runs: on face holds to gain a corner crack

text: Verified 2024 trip report beta: crampons, ice axe, single 70m rope, one set of nuts, cams .2-3 with doubles of 2 and 3. Descent is 14 rappels (5 down the upper West Ridge, 9 down the South Face) — bring extra cord for rap anchors.
runs: rope one set of nuts cams 2 3 with doubles of 2 and 3

text: From the Castle-Pinnacle col, take the obvious east ridge up Pinnacle. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly 4th-class terrain to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-5th-class climbing with an exposed traverse (an old, unreliable piton is present) to a sandy belay bench that has a fixed rappel anchor dropping the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow terrain to the true summit and is often simul-climbed or soloed by comfortable parties. Loose rock and scree are a serious, persistent concern throughout.
runs: a large dead tree pitch 2 is the

text:
From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 miles and about 1,000-1,050 ft to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From there, continue on unmaintained boot path east and behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col. That segment typically takes roughly 2 to 3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain.

The east ridge rises directly from the col. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly fourth-class ground to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-fifth climbing with an exposed traverse to a sandy belay bench carrying a fixed rappel anchor down the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow ground to the true summit, often simul-climbed or soloed.

Loose rock and scree are a serious and repeatedly noted concern throughout.

Descent is either the rappel off the pitch-2 bench down the south face, or over the summit and down the standard south-side scramble to Pinnacle Saddle — the second is only sensible if the leader already knows that line.
runs: a large dead tree pitch 2 is the

text: A crack a couple of feet below the summit bolts is notorious for wedging rope. Stopping at the pitch-3 ledge instead of running the rope through to the top of pitch 2 is the accepted way to avoid it, and is the single most repeated warning on this descent.
runs: a crack a couple of feet below the

text: Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue about half a mile and leave the maintained trail, dropping steeply to cross Thunder Creek, to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). Expect about 8 1/4 miles and 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this camp, roughly 9 hours with an overnight pack. Note: the footbridge that once crossed Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp is gone, so the crossing is a log jam or a wade — check current park trail conditions before you go.
runs: of the lake at the toe of the

text: Most pitches run out beyond 250 feet and are simul-climbed on solid, clean Skagit gneiss. The route favors the right side of the buttress low down, following the rib left of a gully to the top of the first tower, before a crux 8th pitch that combines a chimney, a leftward rising traverse across a face, and an exposed arête requiring careful, sometimes lichen-coated 5.9 moves.
runs: gully to the top of the first tower

text: Take the rib to the left of the gully to the top of the first tower — advice from the first-ascent party to future climbers.
runs: take the rib to the left of the gully to the top of the first tower

text: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before reaching the col, from which the route climbs East Twin Needle's summit block directly above.
runs: 300 below the moraine to the head of crescent creek

text: From the basin camp below Mount Terror around 6,050 ft, head west and drop about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek. Traverse north through Crescent Creek Basin, keeping the party together through the scree to limit rockfall and hugging the cliffs, then make a rising traverse beneath the Eye Col gully that carries you past an adjacent buttress rather than straight up at it. The notch at about 7,400 ft is reached by continuing past a gully that would otherwise force a rappel — that decoy gully is the thing to walk by. The last stretch to the col is scree you walk up rather than rock you climb.
runs: below the moraine to the head of crescent creek

text: From the basin camp below Mount Terror (~6,050'), descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty — this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light.
runs: 300 below the moraine to the head of crescent creek

text: Belay from the east notch and climb up the east side of the spire a short ways, then downclimb a 5.5 crack about 20 ft to reach the ramp.
runs: belay from the east notch and climb up the east side of the spire a short ways then downclimb a 5.5 crack

text: Ascend the ramp up and west to the corner where it ends; set up a belay.
runs: ascend the ramp up and west to the corner where it ends

text: Climb a short slab to a platform leading to a 1-inch crack protected by two fixed pins; joining the crack is 5.6, the crack itself eases to 5.4. The crack leads to a ledge; from there head a little east to the summit.
runs: two fixed pins joining the crack is 5.6 the crack itself
5.4 the crack leads to a ledge from

text: Reach the Monte Cristo townsite on foot or by bike from Barlow Pass, then take the Glacier Basin Trail less than a mile. The spire stands above the trail, roughly 2,000 ft above the basin. When it makes sense, leave the trail and start up toward the base of the ridge — a snowfield early in the season, extremely loose talus once it has gone. Snow or talus leads up a narrowing gully to the lower col, steepening as it goes, commonly 35 to 45 degrees, with the final couloir steeper and more exposed than anything below it. Best done early in the year while the gully still holds snow: melted out it is loose scree badly exposed to rockfall and a poor outing in late summer. Fixed stations exist in the gully and parties have used them to bypass melted-out gaps on the way down.
runs: talus leads up a narrowing gully to the

text: There are two cols, and you rope up at the second one. The snow gully out of Glacier Basin delivers you to the lower col, and that is not where the climbing starts. From it, scramble around the south face on very loose talus to the upper, east notch, and belay there: the first pitch climbs the east side of the spire a short way, then downclimbs a 5.5 crack about twenty feet to a ramp. Two things confirm you are in the right gully on the way up. Where it narrows, a branch heads left and up — that one leads to the northwest ramp of Wilmans Peak, a different objective entirely, and it carries cornices and hanging snow slabs; the left branch at the narrowing is the documented wrong turn. And once the gully is melted out, an old mine shaft sits in it with yellow tailings all around, open enough to look down into. Confirm again at the top: this summit is a table-top barely larger than the three-piton anchor on it. A summit you can walk about on is one of the other spires.
runs: the east side of the spire a short

text: Cams: doubles from tips to #2, plus a single #3 and single #4. Stoppers: single set.
runs: doubles from tips to 2 plus a single 3 and single 4

text: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. The path climbs steeply through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before breaking out onto talus. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulder field, staying climber's right to avoid an unnecessary crossing of Eldorado Creek, until the talus eases into the open, beautiful alpine Eldorado Creek Basin (a common first camp at roughly 5,400–5,600 ft, ~3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead). From the basin, climb up onto a rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft, then drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (an alternate/second camp at 6,100–6,400 ft, with reliable running water). From Roush Basin, ascend broken talus and slabs onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and continue up moderate glacier slopes to a high camp near 7,500–7,800 ft on the Eldorado–Inspiration Glacier saddle, with views of Moraine Lake, McAllister Glacier and Klawatti Glacier. Rope up for glacier travel here — the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers carry real crevasse hazard, worse as the day warms; parties have broken through hidden snow-bridged creek channels even in the lower basins in spring. From high camp, cross the mostly flat Inspiration Glacier aiming for the low gap on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, then follow the ridge/snow arete up to the base of the summit knife-edge. Total gain is roughly 6,700–6,800 ft trailhead-to-summit; guided parties budget 5–7 hours to high camp and another 3–5 hours (6–9 hours total on summit day) from camp to the top.
runs: from the parking area backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road

text: Climb north up the boulder field on cairns, staying climber's right to avoid crossing Eldorado Creek; it can hold snow into early summer. The talus eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (camps 5,400–5,600 ft). Cross the ridge above at about 6,100–6,200 ft into Roush Basin, then take talus and slabs to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; the highest camps sit near the East Ridge at about 7,800 ft.
runs: slabs to the toe of the eldorado glacier

text: From Marblemount, go straight past the last gas station onto Cascade River Road, cross the bridge and drive to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at mile 20, on the right; the last 10 miles are gravel.
runs: and drive to the eldorado creek trailhead at

text:
Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the mountain's northwest side and the wild Marble Creek Cirque. High camp is either in Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek Basin or at the Eldorado-Inspiration site near 7,500-7,600 ft.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch sometimes called the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and rappel from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.
runs: notch between the north ridge and the first rock spire

text:
Once you are in the cirque the route is obvious, and two separate parties say so in nearly the same words: on looking up from below the rappel, one recorded instantly seeing the line — steep, fat and unmistakable. The couloir splits the northwest face and there is nothing else in the cirque it could be confused with. So the navigation problem is not identifying the couloir; it is getting into the cirque at all.

The notch is the thing to find, and it is shared with the North Ridge. It is the obvious gap between the North Ridge and the First Rock Spire, at about 8,100 ft, reached by traversing north from the East Ridge glacier track. At that notch the two routes go opposite ways: rappel down the far side into the cirque and you are on this route; climb steep snow up onto the rock crest and you are on the North Ridge.

The base itself is the transition at about 7,800 ft where the couloir meets the glacier — which is the usual place to find the moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier before you reach it.

One branch point worth knowing: at least one party climbed a steep line just to climber's left of the main gut of the couloir rather than the gut itself. Both go; the gut is the route as described.

Confirm on the climbing: the line runs from about 7,800 ft to about 8,800 ft, roughly 1,000 ft, usually two or three long pitches or simul-climbed blocks, and the character is a succession of short ice steps broken by lower-angle snow rather than one continuous wall. Steps around 70-80 degrees with occasional near-vertical bulges for a body length is right; sustained vertical ice for a full pitch is not this route in any season.
runs: a steep line just to climber's left of the main gut of the couloir

text: Drive State Route 20 (North Cascades Highway) to milepost 126 and turn off at the sign for the village of Diablo, a Seattle City Light company town. Park near the river across from the domed swimming pool; the Sourdough Mountain Trail begins immediately behind the pool building (roughly 890-900 ft). Follow the trail as it switchbacks steeply through forest. At an unmarked junction around 4,300-4,400 ft, leave the maintained trail and head up onto the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge (roughly 6,500 ft) rather than continuing to the Sourdough Mountain Lookout; if you reach the Sourdough Creek crossing and open views of Diablo Lake, you have gone past the turn-off. From the ridge crest, continue along the mostly open, trail-less ridge toward Elephant Butte.
runs: the village of diablo a seattle city light company town

text: Take SR-20 to milepost 126 and turn off at the sign for the village of Diablo (a Seattle City Light company town); park near the river across from the domed swimming pool.
runs: the village of diablo a seattle city light company town

text: From the Diablo trailhead behind the pool building, climb the Sourdough Mountain Trail's switchbacks. The Sourdough Creek crossing lies beyond the turn-off on the way to the lookout, so reaching it means you have gone too far. The turn-off is an unmarked junction somewhere around 4,300 to 4,400 ft — it is given variously between 4,000 and 4,400 ft, so treat the elevation as approximate and the feature as the thing to find. From it, a left turn takes you straight north up the ridge crest immediately west of Sourdough Creek rather than continuing toward the Sourdough Mountain lookout. You break out of the trees just before reaching the crest, at around 6,000 ft. On the ridge, keep on or southwest of the top: the northeast side is very steep.
runs: break out of the trees just before reaching the crest at around 6 000

text: Walk the Hannegan Pass Trail about four minutes to a clearing with a large white boulder perched several hundred feet above, and leave the trail. At the foot of a mossy slab, cut left and up along its base on a faint path, scramble about 30 ft up a gully, then cut hard left through brush into a dry creekbed and follow it up to the white boulder. Switchback up the woods above and cut right to the wall. Ellation starts in the shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, at a bolt near the ground. About an hour and 1,200 ft of gain.
runs: shallow grooves above and left of the single pitch crag

text:
Rappel the line of ascent on a single 70m rope used doubled. The descent is not one continuous rappel line and does not map onto the pitches: five rappels bring you down the main wall to a gear belay at its toe, then you downscramble a 3rd/4th-class gully to the big treed ledge, then three more rappels reach the ground. Seven of the eight are too long for a 60m rope, and the last is 115 ft — the whole reach of a doubled 70 — so knot the ends.

Two stations need naming in advance. The rappel down pitch 6 is where ropes jam: a crack at the top of the ramp catches the pull, and parties have had to re-climb the pitch to free it. Clip the pull strand through a leaver biner on the second bolt below that station and it stops being a problem. And the station off the big treed ledge is a tree on slings, roughly 30-40 ft to climber's left of the top of pitch 3 — the only anchor on the route without fixed metal, so inspect what you find.

From the base, retrace the brushy climbers' path down through timber and mossy slabs to the Hannegan Pass Trail and out to the trailhead.
runs: left of the top of pitch 3 the

text: Start in the series of shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, marked by a bolt near the ground. Climb the bolted groove to a spacious tree ledge. Dirt washes onto this pitch from the ledge above, so expect it to be a little grungy.
runs: series of shallow grooves above and left of the single pitch crag

text: From the tree, hike up and right through brush toward the upper wall and scramble a 4th-class ramp that cuts back left to a bolt just above eye level below a small roof; build a gear belay. Do not take the loose gully that heads up and right from the ledge — it does not reconnect with the route. The pitch goes right on knobs, then up and right on well-bolted face holds, with a few hard moves above the bolts.
runs: a bolt just above eye level below a small roof

text: A slabby 5.7 ramp/corner heads left from the belay: one bolt, then a long stretch where the corner is a seam and the only gear is small hidden placements such as a pocket under a bulge. At the end of the corner, clip a bolt and climb a steep bolted face to the belay. On the rappel this pitch jams ropes.
runs: climb a steep bolted face to the belay

text: Sustained friction climbing, well bolted through the first half with a few small cams in a short flake; the upper part is easier, solid and more runout to the anchor.
runs: with a few small cams in a short flake

text: A boulder move about 10 ft off the anchor on an undercling flake reaches the first bolt; a steep juggy face (2 bolts) leads into a flaring corner where the 5.11a moves are, which can be aided on gear at 5.10 A0. Every move protects well. An easier low-angle crack then slabs out onto the top of the wall.
runs: slabs out onto the top of the wall

text: A bolt low enough to clip from the ground is the confirmation. From the white-boulder clearing, work up to a mossy slab and, standing literally at its base, cut left and up a slight hill on a reasonably well-defined trail running along the foot of the slab. About five minutes of that reaches a dry streambed under a gully. Scramble the gully thirty feet or so, then cut hard left through brush into open forest and a dry creekbed, and follow the creekbed up to a large white boulder. Switchback up the woods above it and cut out to the right once you are 50 to 100 ft from the base of the wall. Ellation starts up a series of shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, and the proof is that bolt near the ground with a couple more on the first pitch. If you are standing at the foot of a single-pitch crag, the route is above and left of you; if you cannot see a bolt near the ground, you are not at the start.
runs: ellation starts up a series of shallow grooves above and left of the single pitch crag

text: Begin at the far end of the treed third-class ledge that slants up and right out of the approach gully. Climb the left-facing corner, a good warm-up on clean rock, to a stance just below a pair of left-slanting twin cracks.
runs: that slants up and right out of the approach gully

text: A light rack suffices for the modest technical difficulty: a handful of stoppers and cams in the 1 to 1.5 inch range, plus several slings; one recorded ascent used only a single stopper for protection through the crux.
runs: cams in the 1 to 1.5 inch range

text: Note the house-sized boulder at the last switchback on the way up; it is your target on the way back down
runs: the house sized boulder at the last switchback

text: From Randle, drive south on Forest Road 25 to Forest Road 2551, just south of Elk Pass, then east on FR2551 for about 1.6 miles to an unmarked spur on the left; park at or just past the spur. From the parking spur, short flagged connector paths lead to the Boundary Trail. Follow the Boundary Trail 2.25 miles to Badger Lake, then continue 2.75 miles and about 700 feet of elevation gain to the last switchback below the ridge crest; from there an almost-level traverse through open timber breaks out onto the open west face of Shark Rock.
runs: miles to an unmarked spur on the left

text: From Randle, drive south on Forest Road 25 to Forest Road 2551, just south of Elk Pass, then east on FR2551 for about 1.6 miles to an unmarked spur on the left; park at or just past the spur.
runs: miles to an unmarked spur on the left

text: Helmet (it is more dangerous to belay than to climb here due to loose rock)
runs: it is more dangerous to belay than to climb

text: A seasonal frozen-waterfall ice climb on Unicorn Peak's northwest face that 'doesn't always form.' From Snow Lake, continue up Unicorn Creek to the base of the northwest face. Pitch 1 is sustained vertical WI5 ice; pitch 2 eases to 50-degree ice; pitch 3 finishes over steep rime and choss to the summit.
runs: from snow lake continue up unicorn creek to the base of the northwest face

text: Drive Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake/Snow Lake trailhead, on the south side of the road about 1.5 miles east of the Reflection Lakes parking area and roughly 3 miles beyond Narada Falls. From the trailhead at about 4,550 ft, follow the Bench Lake/Snow Lake trail 0.75 mile to Bench Lake, then a further 0.5 mile to Snow Lake at 4,685 ft, which sits in a glacial cirque directly below Unicorn Peak. From the lake, continue up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque to the base of the northwest face. Total is roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain from the car to the base of the ice. In winter, when Stevens Canyon Road is gated, add about 3 miles of unplowed road from Narada Falls; one spring party on skis reported four hours from the car to the base of the climbing.
runs: miles east of the reflection lakes parking area

text:
Drive Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake and Snow Lake trailhead, on the south side of the road about 1.5 miles east of the Reflection Lakes parking area. From the trailhead near 4,550 ft, follow the trail 0.75 mile to Bench Lake, then a further half mile to Snow Lake at 4,685 ft, which sits in a glacial cirque directly below the peak.

From the lake, continue up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque to the base of the northwest face. Roughly 1.5 to 2 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain from the car to the base of the ice.

In winter, when Stevens Canyon Road is gated, add about 3 miles of unplowed road from Narada Falls; one spring party on skis reported four hours from the car to the base of the climbing.

There are no fixed anchors on the face. Retreat means threads you build.
runs: miles east of the reflection lakes parking area

text: 1,100 ft (333 m) of technical rock across 8 pitches, plus roughly 500 ft of 3rd-class scrambling to the summit. Climbs wild knobs and diorite fins reminiscent of California granite. Pitches are steep, long, and relatively sustained for alpine climbing; rock quality is generally very good but can be lichen-y/dirty in places from low traffic. Generally very good protection, especially at the cruxes, with a couple of runout sections (pitches 2 and 5).
runs: pitches are steep long and relatively sustained for alpine climbing
generally very good protection especially at the cruxes

text: Descend the Corkscrew line: down-climb a few hundred feet from the gear stash, then a steep heathered gully to an "access ramp"; follow the ramp to a slabby downclimb, with optional rappels down to snow (keeps it 4th class) or continue downclimbing (low 5th).
runs: optional rappels down to snow keeps it 4th

text: Doubles of cams from roughly #0.2 to #2, a single #3, a full set of stoppers, and lots of alpine draws (doubles of slings recommended).
runs: set of stoppers and lots of alpine draws doubles

text: Can be climbed car-to-car in a big day from Seattle, or with a bivy at the base (running water available).
runs: in a big day from seattle or with a bivy at the base

text: Runout sections on pitch 2 and pitch 5 despite generally good protection at the cruxes
runs: runout sections on pitch 2 and pitch 5

text: Generally very good protection, especially at the pitch cruxes, but with runout sections on pitch 2 and pitch 5.

text: Smaller of the two closely-spaced fins at the core of The Dikes; park ~1.5 mi past the trailhead just after the river bridge, cross the road, scramble down the abutment, and follow the trail downstream on the NW bank.
runs: the road scramble down the abutment and follow

text: From the base of Spontaneity Arête, traverse about 250 yards toward the middle of the northwest face on 3rd- and 4th-class ledges to the start. The first pitch is a chimney and hand crack to a large ledge.

chimney and hand crack to a large ledge

text: A hands-and-fists corner, somewhat vegetated, which begins just around the corner from a 5.10 splitter finger crack.
runs: around the corner from a 5.10 splitter finger crack

text: Established by Darin Berdinka on September 11, 2017. Climbs a friction slab past 5 bolts, an easier bolted slab with a fixed pin, a long protectable seam pitch mixing gear and bolts, a short bolted connector pitch, and a final progressively harder face pitch to the top. Rock quality on this part of the face is generally excellent; pitches 1/2 and 3/4 can be readily linked with a 60m rope.
runs: rock quality on this part of the face is generally excellent

text: Scramble a short way up the gully, then climb the dirty low-fifth-class crack/groove on the right side of a brushy wall to reach the foot of Roan Wall. The crack holds moss and dirt and is noticeably worse when wet.
runs: on the right side of a brushy wall

text: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit.
runs: 3 miles to the signed devore creek trail junction

text: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.
runs: up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle
